You know, a lot of people in the whole Reddit free speech debate tend to say "first amendment is only for the government, not businesses" and this is true but not really the point. The point in that case is that Reddit initially sold itself and garnered success by promising to be a platform for free speech and by reeling back on that they are alienating a lot of the users that made the place worth going to in the first place.

Plus we don't all live in the US where the constitution is thought of as some sacred document delivered by god-men, so we don't care about American law analogies. Almost every democratic country has a constitution. All we want is a platform to speak freely and share ideas, which we now have again, so while Reddit are entitled to change their terms of service I won't be supporting them any longer.

Completely agree. Free speech is larger than the First Amendment, which is a trifle unless there is a means of dissemination. Places like Reddit and Voat are modern-day town squares; absolutely essential in political education, activism, and mobilization. Censorship in any form, especially when concentrated in the hands of the powerful and the few, is anathema to an engaged and informed polity. We can wave flags on Memorial Day in honor of those who fought for our freedoms, but if forums for truly free expression cease to exist, there's no point.

Freedom of speech is only meaningful when there are places to speak. Those who rationalize censorship by private actors by reference to the scope of the Bill of Rights are technically correct, but don't understand the operative principles of democracy.

The point in that case is that Reddit initially sold itself and garnered success by promising to be a platform for free speech and by reeling back on that they are alienating a lot of the users that made the place worth going to in the first place.

And as a private business, they're entitled to do so. However, people like Atko are equally entitled to start competitors that directly address Reddit's weak points (such as censorship), and Reddit's users are equally entitled to jump ship if they don't like how Reddit chooses to run their business. I don't see an issue with this.

There's a difference between unethical and illegal.

I think earning millions from your userbase and then suddenly taking a 180 on your fundamental tenets while actively working to suppress discussion of said 180 as you continue to profit from people not in the know is extremely unethical. While I agree that are allowed to do this, I certainly see a major issue with it. I can't really decided on an opinion on whether they ought to be allowed to do this though. Both sides of the argument are extremely compelling.

In any case in the future I imagine this will become a moot point. Peer-To-Peer sites will enable people to take centralized authorities out of the game altogether. Bitcoin, for instance, is an example of doing something which less technically literate people would likely have thought impossible - creating a sort of exchangeable currency with no centralized distributor or bank.

I can't really decided on an opinion on whether they ought to be allowed to do this though.

Well, if you believe in the freedom of choice, then they absolutely should be allowed to do this. And everyone should be allowed to react in an appropriate manner, however they see fit. That's an open market system and our right as consumers in this case is to seek an alternative.

Right, that's definitely one side. However, how would you expect people to be able to react in an appropriate manner without sufficient information? Information that the company itself is actively working to prevent people from seeing?

Yes, THAT is the real problem. When we don't know what's actually happening, I agree, we can't make sound decisions. I've felt that about our democratic republic here in the US for a long time. Information is the real power. And censorship is the real problem because we don't know what's being censored.

However, if all things were equal, our freedom to choose should be the difference maker.

I am not complaing about the content or the politics of the stories, just the writing style. And yes, having such a small number of corporations owning all of the mass media outlets is a disaster. At some point, before the corporations took over, there was an understanding of the journalistic process: someone had a story, a journalist would write it out, sources would be verified, a proofreader would check for gross mistakes, and in the most professional places an editor would revise the story for style. While corporate journalism pushes too far on the "editing" side, where the style has to align with corporate interests, "blog" journalism tends to just be unedited writing - a minimum of proofreading, links instead of sources, and the story itself is usually a story about something that happened elsewhere on the "blogosphere", not even a real world event.
